quote: Anyone reporting sudden chest pains should have been hauled off by an ambulance instantly.
content: This is the essay’s lesson, obtained by the essay’s method. If ambulance non-transport is common and paramedic under-triage of chest pain is documented, then the narrator’s model was wrong and his confusion was a real signal pointing at a real defect — which is what "your strength as a rationalist is your ability to be more confused by fiction than by reality" instructs him to notice. The essay does not claim the confusion identified which falsehood was present; it claims that the feeling of strain should have been treated as data instead of explained away. The annotation supplies a second thing the strain was tracking.

quote: Alas, belief is easier than disbelief
content: The essay’s use of Gilbert is illustrative and the correction narrows it in a way that leaves the case intact. Richter and colleagues found that fast rejection of false statements requires relevant background knowledge; where the reader has none, comprehension proceeds without validation, which is precisely the narrator’s situation on a question about emergency-medicine practice. The essay’s own diagnosis, in the sentence after the one quoted, is that he generated a specific rationalization to protect a model he was attached to — so motivated reasoning is named in the text, not substituted for it. The two accounts describe the same failure at different stages.
